subject: math
title: Ratio Quest: Build a Better Deal
objective: Use equivalent ratios, ratio tables, double number lines, and unit rates to compare real-world deals.

visual.title: Ratio table and double number line
visual.caption: A neon market board comparing two snack packs with ratio tables, double number lines, and unit price callouts.
visual.altText: Two snack deals are shown with matching ratio tables and double number lines. Labels point to equivalent ratios, scale factors, and unit rate.
visual.generationPrompt: Create a bold cyber-neon Grade 6 math teaching diagram that compares two snack deals using ratio tables, double number lines, scale factors, and unit rate labels. Make the labels readable, kid-friendly, and classroom-safe.

teachingSupport.summary: Ratios compare quantities, and unit rates make different-size deals fair to compare.
teachingSupport.description: The app teaches the student to see a ratio as a relationship that can scale, then uses a double number line and table to compare real deals.

diagramCallouts.title: Ratio pair
diagramCallouts.body: A ratio compares two quantities in a specific order, such as dollars to tickets or cups to scoops.

diagramCallouts.title: Scale factor
diagramCallouts.body: Equivalent ratios keep the relationship the same by multiplying both quantities by the same factor.

diagramCallouts.title: Unit rate
diagramCallouts.body: A unit rate tells the amount for one, which makes different-size deals easier to compare.

helperNotes: Ask the learner to say what each number means before calculating.
Use the double number line before the shortcut so the relationship stays visible.
Require a fairness sentence: I chose ___ because each one costs ___ or gives ___.

commonMisunderstandings.mistake: Adding the same number to both quantities and calling it equivalent.
commonMisunderstandings.fix: Use a scale factor and ask whether both quantities were multiplied by the same number.

commonMisunderstandings.mistake: Choosing the lower total price instead of the better unit rate.
commonMisunderstandings.fix: Compare the cost for one item or one unit before deciding which deal is better.
Label the quantities first and keep the same order in the table, line, and sentence.

teachingSupport.confusionPrompt: Write whether you are stuck on what the ratio means, how to scale it, how to use the double number line, or how to find the unit rate.

funTasks: Run a neon market challenge: pick the better snack-pack deal and defend it with a unit rate.
Build a ratio table ladder where each step must keep the same relationship.
Design a fair class reward bundle and prove the best deal with a double number line.

groupHomework.title: Better deal crew
groupHomework.sharedOutcome: Submit a one-page deal comparison with a ratio table, double number line, unit rate, and final recommendation.
groupHomework.parentRole: Let the student gather two real prices, then ask them to explain which deal is better and why.

reward: Earn the Deal Hacker badge after proving a better deal and passing the delayed unit-rate recall.

evidenceMoves.priorKnowledgeCheck: Ask the learner to compare two simple prices, label dollars and items, and divide a whole-number total before teaching ratio language.
evidenceMoves.misconceptionCheck: Check for three likely errors: reversing ratio order, adding instead of scaling, and choosing the lower total price instead of the lower unit rate.
evidenceMoves.manipulativeRationale: Use item cards, price tags, ratio tables, and double number lines because they keep the two related quantities visible before symbolic shortcuts.
evidenceMoves.problemSolvingStrategy: Use the strategy: label quantities, build equivalent rows, reduce to one unit, compare unit rates, then defend the choice in a because sentence.
evidenceMoves.workedExample: Model 6 pencils for $3 as $0.50 per pencil, then compare with a wrong example that picks the lower total price without dividing.
evidenceMoves.examplesAndNonExamples: Compare 2:5 and 4:10 as equivalent ratios, then contrast 2:5 and 4:7 as a non-example that was created by adding instead of scaling.
evidenceMoves.knowledgeConnections: Connect multiplication, division, decimal money, tables, number lines, equivalent fractions, percent, and future proportional relationships.
evidenceMoves.metacognitivePrompt: Plan by labeling the quantities, monitor whether both quantities scaled together, evaluate the unit rate, and explain why the chosen deal is fair.
evidenceMoves.interventionTrigger: If the learner reverses labels, uses additive scaling, or chooses by total price, assign the quantity-labeling and unit-rate reteach before the next quiz.
evidenceMoves.transitionBridge: Grade 6 ratios build from fraction equivalence and prepare learners for proportional relationships, percent, scale drawings, slope, and linear functions.
evidenceMoves.feedbackFrame: Name the correct label or row, identify the first scale or division error, and ask the learner to rewrite one unit-rate sentence before scoring again.

sections.warmup: Look at two snack deals and vote for the better buy before calculating.
sections.teach: A ratio compares two quantities. Equivalent ratios multiply both quantities by the same factor. A unit rate tells the amount for one, so deals can be compared fairly.
sections.guidedPractice: Complete a ratio table, then map the same values onto a double number line before writing the unit rate.
sections.independentPractice: Compare two real-world deals and choose the better one using a labeled unit-rate sentence.
sections.activity: Use the interactive ratio board to scale a recipe, ticket bundle, or snack-pack deal and defend the best choice.
sections.reteach: Return to one ratio pair, label each quantity, and build only two equivalent rows before finding the unit rate.
sections.challenge: Design a new deal that looks cheaper but is not better, then explain the trap.

quiz.prompt: A pack has 6 pencils for $3. What is the cost per pencil?
quiz.explanation: Divide $3 by 6 pencils. Each pencil costs $0.50.

quiz.prompt: Which ratio is equivalent to 2 cups of juice for 5 cups of water?
choices: 4 cups of juice for 10 cups of water
3 cups of juice for 6 cups of water
2 cups of juice for 7 cups of water
5 cups of juice for 2 cups of water
quiz.explanation: Multiplying both 2 and 5 by 2 gives 4 to 10, so the relationship stays the same.

quiz.prompt: Deal A is 4 tickets for $12. Deal B is 6 tickets for $15. Which is the better price per ticket?
quiz.explanation: Deal A is $3 per ticket. Deal B is $2.50 per ticket, so Deal B is the better price.

studentFacing.mission: Hack the neon market by proving which deal is actually better.
studentFacing.whyItMatters: Ratios and unit rates help you make fair comparisons in shopping, recipes, games, speed, maps, and class projects.
studentFacing.bigIdea: Equivalent ratios keep the same relationship, and unit rates compare every deal by one unit.
modelSteps: Label what the two quantities mean and keep the order the same.
Multiply or divide both quantities by the same factor to make equivalent ratios.
Find the amount for one unit, then use that unit rate to compare deals.
studentFacing.example: If 6 pencils cost $3, then 1 pencil costs $0.50 because 3 dollars divided by 6 pencils equals 0.50 dollars per pencil.
studentFacing.nonExample: Adding 2 to both quantities does not usually make an equivalent ratio because the relationship changes.
studentFacing.quickCheck: Before choosing the better deal, say the unit rate for Deal A and Deal B out loud.
studentFacing.studentSummary: A ratio is a relationship. A unit rate makes the relationship easy to compare.
studentFacing.tutorHandoff: Tell the tutor if you are stuck on ratio order, scaling, double number lines, or the unit rate.

learningObjective: Use equivalent ratios, ratio tables, double number lines, and unit rates to compare real-world deals.
successCriteria: I can explain what both quantities in a ratio mean.
I can build equivalent ratios by multiplying or dividing both quantities by the same factor.
I can use a double number line or ratio table to find a unit rate.
I can defend which deal is better using a unit-rate sentence.
essentialQuestion: How can ratios help us compare different-size deals fairly?

knowledge: A ratio compares two quantities in a chosen order.
Equivalent ratios preserve the same relationship by scaling both quantities equally.
A unit rate compares a quantity to one unit.
capability: Build a ratio table from a real-world deal.
Use a double number line to find a unit rate.
Compare two deals with a labeled unit-rate sentence.
reasoning: Detect when a deal looks cheaper because the total price is lower but the unit rate is worse.
Explain why adding the same number to both quantities usually changes the ratio relationship.
retention: Recall the equivalent-ratio rule and unit-rate comparison after a delay.
transfer: Use ratio reasoning on a new shopping, recipe, map, game-currency, or classroom-budget problem.

phaseModules.title: Enter the neon market
phaseModules.studentAction: Pick which snack deal looks better, then write what information you need to prove it.
phaseModules.successCheck: The learner recognizes that a first guess needs fair-comparison evidence.

phaseModules.title: See the relationship
phaseModules.studentAction: Watch the ratio table and double number line show the same relationship in two visual forms.
phaseModules.teacherModel: Label the quantities first, then scale both quantities by the same factor.
phaseModules.visualSupport: A neon market board comparing two snack packs with ratio tables, double number lines, and unit price callouts.
phaseModules.successCheck: The learner can point to the same ratio pair in the table and on the double number line.

phaseModules.title: Break the deal into ratio, scale, and unit rate
phaseModules.studentAction: Sort each part of a worked example into quantity labels, scale factor, equivalent ratio, and unit rate.
phaseModules.teacherModel: The unit rate is the deal reduced to one unit, not just the smallest-looking number.
phaseModules.successCheck: The learner can explain why 4 for $10 and 2 for $5 have the same price per item.

phaseModules.title: Build the better-deal board
phaseModules.studentAction: Complete a ratio table and double number line for two deals, then calculate each unit rate.
phaseModules.teacherModel: Complete a ratio table, then map the same values onto a double number line before writing the unit rate.
phaseModules.successCheck: The learner creates a matching table, line, and unit-rate sentence.

phaseModules.title: Defend the fair comparison
phaseModules.studentAction: Write which deal is better and use because plus two labeled unit rates.
phaseModules.teacherModel: A strong answer says what one unit costs or gives for both deals.
phaseModules.successCheck: The learner explains the choice without relying on total price alone.

phaseModules.title: Complete the deal checkpoint
phaseModules.studentAction: Answer the ratio and unit-rate quiz items independently.
phaseModules.successCheck: The learner completes the checkpoint without final-answer help.

phaseModules.title: Store the comparison rule
phaseModules.studentAction: Return later to recall the rule: scale both quantities together, then compare one unit.
phaseModules.successCheck: Delayed recall is scheduled before durable mastery is claimed.

phaseModules.title: Find a real better deal
phaseModules.studentAction: Use a real or teacher-provided price pair to build a table, line, unit rate, and recommendation.
phaseModules.successCheck: The learner applies ratio reasoning to a changed shopping, recipe, or classroom-budget problem.

phaseModules.title: Choose reteach or challenge
phaseModules.studentAction: If the unit-rate sentence is weak, retry with one labeled ratio; if it is strong, design a misleading deal.
phaseModules.successCheck: The next move is based on evidence from the learner's explanation, not only the score.

proofTasks.prompt: State the rule for creating an equivalent ratio.
Explain why adding the same number to both quantities can break a ratio relationship.
Compare two deals by finding both unit rates.
After a delay, solve a new unit-rate comparison without looking back at the model.
Use ratio reasoning on a new real-world deal, recipe, game-currency, or map-scale problem.

feedbackRules.result: The learner changes the meaning by reversing or mixing quantity order.
feedbackRules.hint: Label the two quantities before writing the ratio, table, or sentence.
feedbackRules.action: Return to the quantity-labeling step and rebuild the first row.

feedbackRules.result: The learner adds the same amount instead of multiplying by the same scale factor.
feedbackRules.hint: Ask what number multiplies both quantities to get the new row.
feedbackRules.action: Use the ratio table ladder and mark the scale factor beside each arrow.

feedbackRules.result: The learner chooses a lower total price without comparing the price for one unit.
feedbackRules.hint: Find the cost for one item in both deals before choosing.
feedbackRules.action: Use the unit-rate sentence frame: Deal ___ is better because one ___ costs ___.

reteachPaths.trigger: The learner cannot say what each number in the ratio means.
reteachPaths.action: Use two-column labels and physical item cards before building a ratio table.

reteachPaths.trigger: The learner compares total prices instead of unit rates.
reteachPaths.action: Reduce each deal to one item or one unit, then compare the unit-rate sentence.

prerequisiteRepairPaths.trigger: The learner cannot divide money values or interpret decimals.
prerequisiteRepairPaths.action: Repair decimal money division with a simpler 2-item or 4-item price before returning to the deal.

challengePaths.trigger: The learner can compare two deals and explain the unit rates independently.
challengePaths.action: Ask the learner to design a misleading deal that looks cheaper but has a worse unit rate.

transferTask.title: Better deal crew board
transferTask.prompt: Submit a one-page deal comparison with a ratio table, double number line, unit rate, and final recommendation.
transferTask.individualAccountability: Each learner submits one unit-rate sentence and one trap they checked for.

parentTeacherNotes: Use this as Bridge Academy Batch 1 math exemplar for ratios and rates. Keep IXL links as reference-only unless the school or parent has approved external use.
accessibilityNotes: Do not rely only on color to connect table rows to double-number-line points.
Provide alt text for the ratio diagram and spoken labels for the two quantities.
Offer sentence frames and calculator accommodations when arithmetic is not the target barrier.
safetyNotes: Do not send students to external IXL links unless staff or parent approval and licensing are in place.
